definition: Truly what it appears to be; real
example: Her genuine interest in the project made everyone want to help her.
origin: From Latin genuinus, meaning native or natural, from the root of gignere, to beget.

definition: Unwilling and hesitant to do something
example: He was reluctant to lend his car to a friend he barely knew.
origin: From Latin reluctari, to struggle against, from re- (against) and luctari (to struggle).

definition: Producing strong, clear images in the mind
example: I still have a vivid memory of my first day at school.
origin: From Latin vividus, meaning lively or full of life, from vivere, to live.

definition: So slight or delicate it is hard to notice
example: There was a subtle hint of lemon in the sauce that I loved.
origin: From Old French sotil, from Latin subtilis, meaning fine, thin or finely woven.

definition: Honest and direct, even when it is uncomfortable
example: In a candid interview, the actor admitted he had nearly quit the film.
origin: From Latin candidus, meaning white or pure, from candere, to shine.

definition: To grow or develop well and successfully
example: Some plants thrive in shade and barely need any direct sunlight.
origin: From Old Norse thrifask, meaning to grasp for oneself or to prosper.

definition: To make progress slow or difficult
example: Heavy snow hindered the rescue team as they climbed toward the cabin.
origin: From Old English hindrian, meaning to harm or hold back, related to the word behind.

definition: Not well known or hard to understand
example: She loves quoting obscure poets that nobody else in the class has read.
origin: From Latin obscurus, meaning dark or dim.

definition: Seeming reasonable and likely to be true
example: His excuse sounded plausible, so the teacher let him hand it in late.
origin: From Latin plausibilis, meaning deserving applause, from plaudere, to applaud.

definition: Long, slow and boring to do
example: Entering all the receipts by hand was a tedious job that took hours.
origin: From Late Latin taediosus, from Latin taedium, meaning weariness or disgust.

definition: Sudden and unexpected, often unpleasantly so
example: The meeting came to an abrupt end when the fire alarm went off.
origin: From Latin abruptus, meaning broken off, from ab- (off) and rumpere (to break).

definition: Clear, logical and easy to follow
example: After a strong coffee she finally managed to give a coherent answer.
origin: From Latin cohaerere, to stick together, from co- (together) and haerere (to stick).

definition: Working carefully and with steady effort
example: A diligent student, he reviewed his notes every evening before dinner.
origin: From Latin diligens, meaning attentive, from diligere, to value highly or love.

definition: Wanting very much to do or have something
example: The children were eager to open their presents before breakfast.
origin: From Old French aigre, meaning sharp or sour, from Latin acer, sharp.

definition: Careful to spend very little money
example: My frugal aunt reuses wrapping paper and never buys anything at full price.
origin: From Latin frugalis, meaning thrifty, from frux, fruit or value.

definition: Unfriendly and showing strong dislike or opposition
example: The crowd turned hostile when the referee cancelled the winning goal.
origin: From Latin hostilis, from hostis, meaning enemy.

definition: Not thinking you are better than others
example: Despite winning three championships, she remained humble and thanked her teammates first.
origin: From Old French, from Latin humilis, meaning low or lowly, from humus, ground.

definition: Clearly expressed and easy to understand
example: Her lucid explanation made the tax rules seem almost simple.
origin: From Latin lucidus, meaning bright or clear, from lux, light.

definition: Ordinary and dull; part of everyday life
example: He listens to podcasts to get through mundane chores like folding laundry.
origin: From Latin mundanus, meaning of the world, from mundus, world.

definition: New and unlike anything seen before
example: The engineers found a novel way to cool the battery without fans.
origin: From Old French novel, from Latin novellus, a diminutive of novus, meaning new.

definition: Acting with care and thought for the future
example: It would be prudent to save some money before quitting your job.
origin: From Latin prudens, a shortened form of providens, meaning foreseeing.

definition: Stiff and unable to bend or change
example: The school has rigid rules about phones that students find frustrating.
origin: From Latin rigidus, meaning stiff, from rigere, to be stiff.

definition: Strong, healthy and unlikely to break or fail
example: We need a robust backup system that keeps working during power cuts.
origin: From Latin robustus, meaning strong like oak, from robur, oak or strength.

definition: Hard to find because there is very little
example: Fresh water became scarce after three months without any rain.
origin: From Old North French escars, from a Vulgar Latin form of Latin excerpere, to pluck out.

definition: Honestly meaning what you say and feel
example: He offered a sincere apology and promised it would not happen again.
origin: From Latin sincerus, meaning pure, clean or whole.

definition: Nervous, strained and unable to relax
example: Everyone in the waiting room was tense as the results were announced.
origin: From Latin tensus, the past participle of tendere, meaning to stretch.

definition: Not clear, exact or fully explained
example: She gave only a vague answer when I asked where she had been.
origin: From Latin vagus, meaning wandering or uncertain.

definition: Very tired after long effort or strain
example: The weary hikers dropped their packs and collapsed beside the campfire.
origin: From Old English werig, meaning tired.

definition: Clever and funny with words
example: Her witty replies on the panel show had the whole audience laughing.
origin: From Old English wittig, meaning wise or clever, from witt, understanding or mind.

definition: Willing to take risks; brave and confident
example: Leaving a secure job to start a bakery was a bold move.
origin: From Old English beald, meaning brave or confident.

definition: Cold, empty and offering little hope
example: The job market looked bleak for graduates during the recession.
origin: From Old Norse bleikr, meaning pale or white.

definition: Quick, energetic and full of life
example: We took a brisk walk around the lake to warm up before lunch.
origin: Of uncertain origin.

definition: To force someone to do something
example: The new law compels companies to report any data breach within three days.
origin: From Latin compellere, to drive together, from com- (together) and pellere (to drive).

definition: Saying a lot clearly in few words
example: Keep your cover letter concise so the recruiter actually reads all of it.
origin: From Latin concisus, meaning cut up or brief, from com- and caedere, to cut.

definition: To discourage someone from doing something
example: Bright lights around the house can deter burglars from trying the doors.
origin: From Latin deterrere, to frighten away, from de- (away) and terrere (to frighten).

definition: To suffer something difficult patiently for a long time
example: The villagers endured months of flooding before help finally arrived.
origin: From Old French endurer, from Latin indurare, to harden, from durus, hard.

definition: To encourage something to grow or develop
example: Good managers foster trust by listening to their teams and keeping promises.
origin: From Old English fostrian, to nourish, from fostor, meaning food.

definition: To take firm hold of or fully understand
example: It took me a while to grasp how the new software actually works.
origin: From Middle English graspen, to reach for or grope, related to Old English grapian, to touch.

definition: Done too quickly and without enough thought
example: Don't make a hasty decision about the house; sleep on it first.
origin: From Old French hastif, from haste, meaning urgency, a word of Germanic origin.

definition: Not strict when punishing or enforcing rules
example: The judge was lenient because it was the teenager's first offense.
origin: From Latin leniens, from lenire, to soften, from lenis, mild or gentle.

definition: Very small in amount; barely enough
example: They survived the winter on a meager supply of rice and beans.
origin: From Old French maigre, meaning thin, from Latin macer, lean.

definition: Too trusting because of little life experience
example: I was naive enough to believe the email promising me free money.
origin: From French naïve, from Latin nativus, meaning native or natural.

definition: An idea, belief or impression about something
example: She rejected the notion that success depends only on talent.
origin: From Latin notio, meaning concept or idea, from noscere, to come to know.

definition: To leave something out, by choice or mistake
example: Please don't omit your phone number when you fill in the form.
origin: From Latin omittere, to let go, from ob- and mittere, to send.

definition: To think about something carefully and at length
example: He sat by the window and pondered whether to accept the offer.
origin: From Latin ponderare, to weigh, from pondus, meaning weight.

definition: Charming in an unusual, old-fashioned way
example: We stayed in a quaint fishing village with cobbled streets and tiny shops.
origin: From Old French cointe, meaning clever or pretty, from Latin cognitus, known.

definition: To prove that a claim is wrong
example: The lawyer used phone records to refute the witness's version of events.
origin: From Latin refutare, meaning to drive back or rebut.

definition: Calm, peaceful and completely untroubled
example: The lake was serene at dawn, without a single ripple on the water.
origin: From Latin serenus, meaning clear or calm, first said of the sky and weather.

definition: Doubting that something is true or useful
example: Doctors were skeptical about the diet until the trial results came in.
origin: From Greek skeptikos, meaning inquiring, from skeptesthai, to look or consider.

definition: Refusing to change your mind or give way
example: My stubborn grandfather still refuses to use a mobile phone.
origin: Of uncertain origin.

definition: Strongly built and not easily damaged
example: You will need sturdy boots for a trail this rocky and steep.
origin: From Old French estourdi, meaning dazed or reckless; the sense of strongly built came later in English.

definition: Happening or moving very quickly
example: The company's swift response to the outage impressed its customers.
origin: From Old English swift, “moving quickly”, related to swifan, “to move in a course, sweep”.

definition: Real enough to be touched or clearly seen
example: After months of training, she finally saw tangible improvement in her running times.
origin: From Late Latin tangibilis, from Latin tangere, “to touch”.

definition: Done with great care and attention to every detail
example: The mechanic gave the car a thorough inspection before the long road trip.
origin: From Old English thuruh, a variant of “through”, with the sense of going from end to end.

definition: Of very little importance or value
example: They argued for an hour over a trivial detail in the seating plan.
origin: From Latin trivialis, “commonplace”, from trivium, “a place where three roads meet”.

definition: To support or defend a rule, decision, or principle
example: The appeals court voted to uphold the original ruling against the company.
origin: Formed in Middle English from up + hold, literally “to hold up”.

definition: Absolutely necessary; essential for life or success
example: Clean water is vital to the health of every community.
origin: From Latin vitalis, “of life”, from vita, “life”.

definition: Cautious about possible dangers or problems
example: After the scam, he became wary of emails asking for his password.
origin: From the older English word ware, “careful, aware”, from Old English waer, “prudent, watchful”.

definition: To want something very much, often with sadness
example: After years in the city, she began to yearn for quiet mountain mornings.
origin: From Old English giernan, “to strive for, desire”, from georn, “eager”.

definition: Great energy and enthusiasm for a cause or goal
example: The new volunteers tackled the beach cleanup with remarkable zeal.
origin: From Greek zelos, “ardor, eager rivalry”, by way of Late Latin zelus.

definition: Lasting for a very short time
example: Online fame is often ephemeral, fading as soon as the next trend arrives.
origin: From Greek ephemeros, “lasting only a day”, from epi, “on”, and hemera, “day”.

definition: Not giving up easily; very determined
example: The tenacious reporter kept calling until the mayor finally agreed to an interview.
origin: From Latin tenax, “holding fast”, from tenere, “to hold”.

definition: Able to express ideas clearly and persuasively
example: Her eloquent speech moved the entire audience to tears.
origin: From Latin eloquens, from eloqui, “to speak out” (e-, “out”, + loqui, “to speak”).

definition: Able to recover quickly from difficulty or setbacks
example: Children are often more resilient than adults expect after a big move.
origin: From Latin resilire, “to leap back”, from re-, “back”, and salire, “to jump”.

definition: Showing extreme care about small details
example: He kept meticulous records of every expense during the renovation.
origin: From Latin meticulosus, “fearful”, from metus, “fear”; the sense later shifted to “anxiously careful”.

definition: Having mixed or conflicting feelings about something
example: She felt ambivalent about the promotion because it meant moving abroad.
origin: From German Ambivalenz, coined by psychiatrist Eugen Bleuler around 1910 from Latin ambi-, “both”, and valentia, “strength”.

definition: Dealing with problems in a practical, sensible way
example: We took a pragmatic approach and fixed the cheapest problems first.
origin: From Greek pragmatikos, “fit for business”, from pragma, “deed, thing done”.

definition: The quality of being open and honest
example: I appreciated her candor when she told me the plan would not work.
origin: From Latin candor, “whiteness, brightness, purity”, from candere, “to shine”.

definition: Severely plain and simple, without comfort or decoration
example: The monk lived in an austere room with only a bed and a desk.
origin: From Greek austeros, “harsh, bitter”, literally “making the tongue dry”, by way of Latin austerus.

definition: Kind and wanting to do good for others
example: A benevolent neighbor paid for the family's groceries all winter.
origin: From Latin bene, “well”, and volens, “wishing”, from velle, “to wish”.

definition: Changing mood or behavior suddenly and without reason
example: The capricious weather ruined our picnic three weekends in a row.
origin: From French capricieux, from Italian capriccio, “a sudden start or whim”.

definition: Too satisfied with yourself to see possible dangers
example: After three easy wins, the team grew complacent and lost badly.
origin: From Latin complacere, “to please greatly”, from com-, an intensifier, and placere, “to please”.

definition: A confusing problem that is hard to solve
example: How to cut costs without losing staff was a real conundrum for the board.
origin: Of uncertain origin; it appeared in English in the late 1500s, possibly as mock-Latin university slang.

definition: Having a hidden meaning that is hard to understand
example: He left a cryptic note on the fridge that nobody could figure out.
origin: From Greek kryptikos, from kryptos, “hidden”.

definition: Seeming so difficult that it makes you nervous
example: Learning a new language at fifty felt daunting, but she enrolled anyway.
origin: From the verb daunt, from Old French danter, from Latin domitare, “to tame”.

definition: A sudden and complete failure or disaster
example: The product launch turned into a debacle when the website crashed.
origin: From French débâcle, “the breaking up of ice in a river”, from débâcler, “to unbar”.

definition: Shy and lacking confidence in your own abilities
example: The diffident new hire rarely spoke up in meetings despite his good ideas.
origin: From Latin diffidere, “to mistrust”, from dis-, “away”, and fidere, “to trust”.

definition: Very different from each other; hard to compare
example: The festival brought together disparate styles, from jazz to heavy metal.
origin: From Latin disparatus, past participle of disparare, “to separate”, from dis-, “apart”, and parare, “to prepare”.

definition: Insisting your beliefs are right without considering others
example: He was so dogmatic about his diet that dinner parties became awkward.
origin: From Greek dogma, “opinion, tenet”, from dokein, “to seem, to think”.

definition: Hard to find, catch, or achieve
example: A good night's sleep remained elusive during the noisy construction next door.
origin: From Latin eludere, “to escape from, to outplay”, from e-, “out”, and ludere, “to play”.

definition: To try to match someone you admire
example: Young players often emulate the stars they watch on television.
origin: From Latin aemulari, “to rival, strive to equal”, from aemulus, “rival”.

definition: A person or thing that is mysterious and puzzling
example: Even after ten years as neighbors, he remained an enigma to us.
origin: From Greek ainigma, “riddle”, from ainissesthai, “to speak in riddles”, from ainos, “fable”.

definition: Not regular or predictable in movement or behavior
example: His erratic driving made the passengers grip their seats.
origin: From Latin erraticus, “wandering”, from errare, “to wander, stray”.

definition: To make a bad situation even worse
example: Skipping meals and sleep will only exacerbate your headaches.
origin: From Latin exacerbare, “to irritate”, from ex-, “thoroughly”, and acerbus, “harsh, bitter”.

definition: Very fussy about details, cleanliness, or accuracy
example: She is fastidious about her kitchen and wipes every counter twice.
origin: From Latin fastidiosus, “disdainful, squeamish”, from fastidium, “loathing”.

definition: Having or showing very strong, sincere feeling
example: He has been a fervent supporter of the local football club since childhood.
origin: From Latin fervens, from fervere, “to boil, glow”.

definition: Having no chance of producing a useful result
example: Arguing with the referee proved futile, and the goal still counted.
origin: From Latin futilis, “leaky, worthless”, literally “pouring out easily”.

definition: Talking too much, especially about unimportant things
example: Our garrulous taxi driver told us his life story before we reached the airport.
origin: From Latin garrulus, from garrire, “to chatter”.

definition: Enjoying the company of other people; sociable
example: My gregarious sister makes friends within minutes at any party.
origin: From Latin gregarius, “belonging to a flock”, from grex, “flock, herd”.

definition: Used so often that it no longer feels fresh
example: The movie relied on hackneyed jokes that everyone had heard before.
origin: From hackney, a horse kept for hire and so overworked, named after Hackney, now part of London.

definition: Perfect, with no faults or mistakes
example: The hotel's service was impeccable from our arrival to our departure.
origin: From Latin impeccabilis, “not liable to sin”, from in-, “not”, and peccare, “to sin”.

definition: Continuing without stopping, often in an annoying way
example: The incessant barking from next door kept us awake all night.
origin: From Late Latin incessans, from in-, “not”, and cessare, “to cease”.

definition: Wanting to avoid effort; habitually lazy
example: The heat made everyone indolent, and nothing got done that afternoon.
origin: From Late Latin indolens, “feeling no pain”, from in-, “not”, and dolere, “to suffer pain”.

definition: Having or showing no skill; clumsy
example: His inept attempt at fixing the sink flooded the whole kitchen.
origin: From Latin ineptus, “unsuitable, absurd”, from in-, “not”, and aptus, “fit”.

definition: Present from birth rather than learned
example: She has an innate sense of rhythm that no teacher could give her.
origin: From Latin innatus, “inborn”, from in-, “in”, and nasci, “to be born”.

definition: Lacking flavor, interest, or energy; dull
example: The soup was so insipid that even extra salt could not save it.
origin: From Late Latin insipidus, “tasteless”, from in-, “not”, and sapidus, “tasty”, from sapere, “to taste”.

definition: Fearless and adventurous in the face of danger
example: The intrepid hikers crossed the glacier despite the approaching storm.
origin: From Latin intrepidus, from in-, “not”, and trepidus, “alarmed”.

definition: Cheerful, friendly, and full of good humor
example: Our jovial host greeted every guest with a laugh and a hug.
origin: From Late Latin jovialis, “of Jupiter”, since people born under that planet were thought to be cheerful.

definition: Showing good sense in making decisions
example: A judicious use of spices can transform a simple dish.
origin: From French judicieux, from Latin judicium, “judgment”, from judex, “judge”.

definition: To express deep sadness or regret about something
example: Fans still lament the closing of the old cinema downtown.
origin: From Latin lamentari, “to wail, moan”, from lamentum, “a wailing”.

definition: Lacking energy and slow to move or act
example: I always feel lethargic after eating a heavy lunch at my desk.
origin: From Greek lethargos, “forgetful”, from lethe, “forgetfulness”, and argos, “idle”.

definition: Tending to talk a great deal
example: The usually quiet professor turned loquacious when asked about her research.
origin: From Latin loquax, “talkative”, from loqui, “to speak”.

definition: Easily shaped or influenced without breaking
example: Gold is so malleable that it can be hammered into sheets thinner than paper.
origin: From medieval Latin malleabilis, “able to be hammered,” from Latin malleus, “hammer.”

definition: To make something less severe or harmful
example: Planting trees along the river helped mitigate the damage from seasonal flooding.
origin: From Latin mitigare, “to soften,” from mitis, “mild, gentle.”

definition: Gloomy, sullen, and unwilling to talk
example: He grew morose after the layoffs and barely spoke to anyone at lunch.
origin: From Latin morosus, “peevish, hard to please,” from mos, “manner, habit.”

definition: Calm and relaxed, as if not concerned
example: She gave a nonchalant shrug when asked about the interview she had just aced.
origin: From French nonchalant, from non, “not,” and chaloir, “to care,” ultimately from Latin calere, “to be warm.”

definition: A warm, wistful longing for the past
example: The smell of fresh bread filled him with nostalgia for his grandmother's kitchen.
origin: Coined in 1688 by Swiss physician Johannes Hofer from Greek nostos, “homecoming,” and algos, “pain.”

definition: A small, subtle difference in meaning or tone
example: A good translator captures every nuance of the original author's voice.
origin: From French nuance, “shade of color,” from nue, “cloud,” from Latin nubes.

definition: Stubbornly refusing to change one's mind
example: The obstinate toddler refused to wear a coat despite the freezing wind.
origin: From Latin obstinatus, past participle of obstinare, “to persist, stand firm.”

definition: Suggesting that something bad will happen
example: Ominous dark clouds gathered over the stadium just before the match began.
origin: From Latin ominosus, from omen, “a sign of what is to come.”

definition: Richly luxurious and showing great wealth
example: The hotel lobby was opulent, with marble floors and crystal chandeliers overhead.
origin: From Latin opulentus, “wealthy,” from ops, “wealth, resources.”

definition: Showy in a way meant to impress
example: He arrived in an ostentatious gold sports car that nobody could ignore.
origin: From Latin ostentare, “to display,” an intensive form of ostendere, “to show.”

definition: A statement that seems contradictory yet may be true
example: It is a paradox that the more choices we have, the less satisfied we feel.
origin: From Greek paradoxos, “contrary to expectation,” from para, “beyond,” and doxa, “opinion.”

definition: A smallness of amount; not enough of something
example: The paucity of evidence forced the detectives to close the case.
origin: From Latin paucitas, from paucus, “few, little.”

definition: Deep in quiet, often slightly sad thought
example: She sat by the window, pensive, watching the rain streak down the glass.
origin: From Old French pensif, from penser, “to think,” from Latin pensare, “to weigh, consider.”

definition: Spreading widely through every part of something
example: The pervasive smell of smoke lingered in the house for weeks after the fire.
origin: From Latin pervadere, “to go through,” from per, “through,” and vadere, “to go.”

definition: Calm and peaceful, not easily upset
example: The lake was so placid at dawn that it mirrored the mountains perfectly.
origin: From Latin placidus, “gentle, calm,” from placere, “to please.”

definition: Touching the emotions deeply, often with sadness
example: The film ends with a poignant scene of the soldier reading his daughter's letter.
origin: From Old French poignant, “pricking,” from poindre, from Latin pungere, “to prick, sting.”

definition: Dangerously unstable or likely to fall or fail
example: The ladder stood at a precarious angle against the icy roof.
origin: From Latin precarius, “obtained by begging,” and so dependent on another's favor, from prex, “prayer.”

definition: Producing a great deal of work or offspring
example: The prolific novelist published three books in a single year.
origin: From medieval Latin prolificus, from Latin proles, “offspring,” and facere, “to make.”

definition: A state of uncertainty over a difficult choice
example: Two great job offers left her in a quandary about where to live.
origin: Of uncertain origin.

definition: Deep, long-lasting bitterness or resentment
example: Years after the divorce, they could finally talk to each other without rancor.
origin: From Late Latin rancor, “rancidness, bitterness,” from Latin rancere, “to stink, be rancid.”

definition: Unwilling to speak freely or share thoughts
example: He was reticent about his past and changed the subject whenever it came up.
origin: From Latin reticere, “to keep silent,” from re-, an intensifier, and tacere, “to be silent.”

definition: To feel deep respect and admiration for
example: Students revere the old professor for her wisdom and kindness.
origin: From Latin revereri, “to stand in awe of,” from re-, an intensifier, and vereri, “to fear, respect.”

definition: Showing keen judgment and deep wisdom
example: Her sagacious advice saved the company from a disastrous merger.
origin: From Latin sagax, “keen-scented, quick to perceive.”

definition: To examine something very closely and carefully
example: Auditors scrutinized every receipt before approving the expense report.
origin: From Latin scrutinium, “a search,” from scrutari, “to search, examine,” originally to sort through scruta, “rubbish.”

definition: The luck of making pleasant discoveries by chance
example: By pure serendipity, she met her future business partner on a delayed flight.
origin: Coined by Horace Walpole in 1754 from the Persian tale The Three Princes of Serendip, Serendip being an old name for Sri Lanka.

definition: Comfort found in a time of sadness
example: After the funeral, he found solace in long walks along the beach.
origin: From Old French solas, from Latin solacium, from solari, “to console.”

definition: To waste money, time, or a chance foolishly
example: He squandered his entire inheritance on gambling within two years.
origin: Of uncertain origin.

definition: Enduring pain or hardship without complaining
example: She stayed stoic through the long treatment, never letting her fear show.
origin: From Greek stoa, “porch,” after the Painted Porch in Athens where the philosopher Zeno taught.

definition: Expressed clearly in very few words
example: Keep your summary succinct; the board has only five minutes to read it.
origin: From Latin succinctus, “tucked up,” from sub, “under,” and cingere, “to gird.”

definition: More than is needed; unnecessary
example: The editor cut every superfluous word until the essay fit on one page.
origin: From Latin superfluus, “overflowing,” from super, “over,” and fluere, “to flow.”

definition: Saying very little; quiet by nature
example: Our taciturn neighbor nods hello but has never spoken a full sentence to us.
origin: From Latin taciturnus, from tacitus, “silent,” from tacere, “to be silent.”

definition: Very weak, thin, or slight; easily broken
example: The link between the suspect and the crime was tenuous at best.
origin: From Latin tenuis, “thin.”

definition: A feeling of fear about what may happen
example: With some trepidation, she opened the envelope containing her exam results.
origin: From Latin trepidare, “to tremble, be agitated,” from trepidus, “alarmed.”

definition: Seeming to be found everywhere at once
example: Smartphones have become so ubiquitous that public payphones have almost vanished.
origin: From Latin ubique, “everywhere,” from ubi, “where.”

definition: To honor with deep, almost religious respect
example: Many cultures venerate their elders and seek their guidance on major decisions.
origin: From Latin venerari, “to worship, revere,” from venus, “love, desire.”

definition: To prove someone right or clear of blame
example: New DNA evidence vindicated the man after twelve years in prison.
origin: From Latin vindicare, “to claim, avenge, set free,” from vindex, “claimant, avenger.”

definition: Likely to change suddenly and unpredictably
example: Investors are nervous because the stock market has been volatile all month.
origin: From Latin volatilis, “flying, fleeting,” from volare, “to fly.”

definition: Playfully odd or fanciful in an appealing way
example: The café is decorated with whimsical teapots shaped like animals.
origin: From whim, a shortening of the older English whim-wham, “fanciful object,” itself of unknown origin.

definition: Idealistic in a wildly impractical way
example: His quixotic plan to end traffic by giving everyone a bicycle amused the council.
origin: From Don Quixote, the deluded, chivalry-obsessed hero of Miguel de Cervantes's novel, first published in 1605.

definition: Having a mysterious, spiritual, or holy quality
example: Standing alone in the ancient cathedral, she felt a numinous presence around her.
origin: From Latin numen, “divine will,” literally “a nod” of a god.

definition: Long, hard study or writing, especially at night
example: Her thesis was the product of months of late-night lucubration in the library.
origin: From Latin lucubrare, “to work by lamplight,” from lux, “light.”

definition: A person who loves words
example: A true logophile, he reads the dictionary for fun on weekends.
origin: From Greek logos, “word,” and philos, “loving.”

definition: The pleasant earthy smell of rain on dry ground
example: After weeks of drought, the petrichor rising from the garden felt like a gift.
origin: Coined in 1964 by Australian scientists Isabel Bear and Richard Thomas from Greek petra, “stone,” and ichor, the fluid in the veins of the gods.

definition: Sweet and smooth to hear, like honey
example: The narrator's mellifluous voice made even the tax documentary a pleasure to hear.
origin: From Latin mellifluus, from mel, “honey,” and fluere, “to flow.”

definition: Quick to notice and understand things clearly
example: A perspicacious editor spotted the plot flaw that everyone else had missed.
origin: From Latin perspicax, “sharp-sighted,” from perspicere, “to see through.”

definition: Too eager to please or obey someone
example: The obsequious waiter laughed at every joke the wealthy customer made.
origin: From Latin obsequiosus, “compliant,” from obsequi, “to comply,” from ob, “toward,” and sequi, “to follow.”

definition: Lacking courage; timid and easily frightened
example: The pusillanimous manager refused to defend his team when the director blamed them.
origin: From Latin pusillus, “very small,” and animus, “spirit, mind.”

definition: Stubbornly resisting authority or control
example: The recalcitrant mule refused to move no matter how hard the farmer pulled.
origin: From Latin recalcitrare, “to kick back,” from calx, “heel.”

definition: Someone who flatters powerful people to gain favor
example: The CEO surrounded himself with sycophants who praised every bad idea he had.
origin: From Greek sykophantes, “informer, slanderer,” apparently from sykon, “fig,” and phainein, “to show.”

definition: Quick to argue or fight; aggressively defiant
example: The truculent passenger shouted at the crew when asked to stow his bag.
origin: From Latin truculentus, from trux, “fierce, savage.”

definition: A change of fortune, usually an unwelcome one
example: Their friendship survived every vicissitude of war, illness, and distance.
origin: From Latin vicissitudo, from vicissim, “in turn,” from vicis, “a turn, change.”

definition: Great physical beauty, especially of a person
example: The magazine praised the actor's pulchritude but said little about his talent.
origin: From Latin pulchritudo, from pulcher, meaning “beautiful”.

definition: To make something deliberately unclear or hard to understand
example: The company used dense legal jargon to obfuscate the real cost of the loan.
origin: From Late Latin obfuscare, “to darken”, from ob- “over” and fuscus “dark”.

definition: Relaxed and unworried, showing a casual lack of concern
example: She gave an insouciant shrug and walked into the exam without any notes.
origin: From French insouciant, from in- “not” and soucier “to worry”, ultimately from Latin sollicitare “to disturb”.

definition: Using very few words to say something
example: His laconic reply to my three-page email was a single word: fine.
origin: From Greek Lakonikos, “of Laconia”, the region around Sparta, whose people were famous for their terse speech.

definition: Generous and forgiving, especially toward a rival or enemy
example: The champion was magnanimous in victory, praising her opponent's skill and courage.
origin: From Latin magnanimus, from magnus “great” and animus “soul, spirit”.

definition: Not telling the truth; habitually dishonest
example: The mendacious salesman swore the used car had never been in an accident.
origin: From Latin mendax (stem mendac-), meaning “lying”, related to mendum “fault”.

definition: Extremely generous, especially in giving money or gifts
example: A munificent donation from a former student paid for the new library.
origin: From Latin munificus, from munus “gift” and facere “to make”.

definition: Wicked or criminal in a shocking way
example: Police uncovered a nefarious scheme to steal the savings of elderly residents.
origin: From Latin nefarius, from nefas “wrong, crime”, from ne- “not” and fas “divine law”.

definition: Stubbornly refusing to change one's mind or feelings
example: Despite hours of pleading, the landlord remained obdurate and refused to lower the rent.
origin: From Latin obduratus, past participle of obdurare “to harden”, from durus “hard”.

definition: Extremely unwilling to spend money or use resources
example: My parsimonious uncle reuses tea bags and never turns on the heating.
origin: From Latin parsimonia “thrift”, from parcere “to spare”.

definition: Very clear, either to see through or to understand
example: Her pellucid explanation made quantum physics seem almost simple to the whole class.
origin: From Latin pellucidus, from perlucere “to shine through”, from per “through” and lucere “to shine”.

definition: Done quickly and carelessly, without real interest or effort
example: The guard gave my bag a perfunctory glance and waved me through.
origin: From Late Latin perfunctorius “careless”, from Latin perfungi “to get through with, discharge”.

definition: Causing serious harm, often slowly and without being noticed
example: The pernicious rumor spread quietly online and eventually ruined her reputation.
origin: From Latin perniciosus, from pernicies “ruin”, from per- “completely” and nex “death”.

definition: Calm and not easily excited or upset
example: The phlegmatic pilot announced the engine trouble as if reading a weather report.
origin: From Greek phlegmatikos, from phlegma “phlegm”, the bodily humor once believed to cause a calm, sluggish temperament.

definition: Complaining in a whining, irritable way
example: The querulous passenger grumbled about the seat, the food, and the delay.
origin: From Latin querulus, from queri “to complain”.

definition: Cheerfully hopeful, especially in a difficult situation
example: Despite falling sales, the founder remains sanguine about the company's future.
origin: From Latin sanguineus “of blood”, from sanguis “blood”; in medieval medicine a temperament ruled by blood was thought to be cheerful.

definition: Using very long words; long-winded
example: The professor's sesquipedalian lectures sent students reaching for their dictionaries.
origin: From Latin sesquipedalis, “a foot and a half long”, a term the poet Horace used to mock overly long words.

definition: Tending to make a person feel sleepy
example: The warm room and the speaker's soporific voice had half the audience nodding off.
origin: From Latin sopor “deep sleep” combined with -ficus “making”, from facere “to make”.

definition: Seeming true or right but actually false
example: The ad relied on the specious claim that expensive vitamins prevent every illness.
origin: From Latin speciosus “beautiful, plausible”, from species “appearance”.

definition: Behaving as if one is better than others
example: The supercilious waiter raised an eyebrow when we ordered the cheapest wine.
origin: From Latin superciliosus, from supercilium “eyebrow”, from super “above” and cilium “eyelid”.

definition: Done secretly to avoid being noticed
example: He took a surreptitious look at his phone during the long meeting.
origin: From Latin surrepticius, from surripere “to seize secretly”, from sub “under” and rapere “to seize”.

definition: Strongly favoring one side of an argument; biased
example: The documentary was so tendentious that it ignored every fact against its case.
origin: From German tendenziös, from Tendenz “tendency”, ultimately from Latin tendere “to stretch”.

definition: Sharp, forceful, and clear in expressing ideas
example: Her trenchant review exposed every weakness in the film's plot.
origin: From Old French trenchant “cutting”, the present participle of trenchier “to cut”.

definition: Insincerely flattering in an oily, overly smooth way
example: The unctuous host praised every guest while clearly angling for donations.
origin: From Medieval Latin unctuosus, from Latin unctus “anointing”, from unguere “to anoint”.

definition: The quality of seeming true or real
example: Real street names and local slang give the novel a strong sense of verisimilitude.
origin: From Latin verisimilitudo, from verus “true” and similis “like”.

definition: To criticize someone using harsh, abusive language
example: Callers phoned the radio show to vituperate the mayor over the tax increase.
origin: From Latin vituperare “to blame”, from vitium “fault” and parare “to prepare”.

definition: Difficult to understand because it is complicated or obscure
example: The lecture on abstruse tax law left most of the audience baffled.
origin: From Latin abstrusus “hidden”, past participle of abstrudere “to conceal”, from ab- “away” and trudere “to push”.

definition: Full of anger, bitterness, and harsh words
example: After an acrimonious divorce, the couple communicated only through their lawyers.
origin: From Latin acrimonia “sharpness”, from acer “sharp”.

definition: Cheerful eagerness and speed in doing something
example: She accepted the job offer with alacrity and started the following Monday.
origin: From Latin alacritas, from alacer “lively, eager”.

definition: Something or someone that is intensely disliked
example: Wasting food was anathema to my grandmother, who grew up during the war.
origin: From Greek anathema, “a thing devoted”, later “a thing devoted to evil”, from anatithenai “to set up”.

definition: Widely told but probably not true
example: The story that he invented the dish by accident is almost certainly apocryphal.
origin: From Greek apokryphos “hidden”, from apokryptein “to hide away”.

definition: Working with great care, effort, and persistence
example: An assiduous researcher, she checked every source twice before publishing.
origin: From Latin assiduus, from assidere “to sit beside, attend to”, from ad “to” and sedere “to sit”.

definition: Eager to fight or start a conflict
example: The president's bellicose speech raised fears of war in the region.
origin: From Latin bellicosus, from bellum “war”.

definition: A harsh, unpleasant mixture of loud sounds
example: A cacophony of car horns and jackhammers greeted us outside the hotel.
origin: From Greek kakophonia, from kakos “bad” and phone “sound”.

definition: Rude, unfriendly, and bad-tempered
example: It would be churlish to refuse such a kind and generous invitation.
origin: From Old English ceorl, “peasant, man of low rank”.

definition: Using many words where fewer would do
example: After ten minutes of circumlocution, the minister still had not answered the question.
origin: From Latin circumlocutio, from circum “around” and loqui “to speak”.

definition: Clear, logical, and convincing
example: She presented a cogent argument for moving the company's headquarters to Denver.
origin: From Latin cogere “to drive together, compel”, from co- “together” and agere “to drive”.

definition: Feeling or showing deep regret for doing wrong
example: The contrite teenager apologized and offered to pay for the broken window.
origin: From Latin contritus “ground to pieces”, from conterere “to grind”, from terere “to rub”.

definition: Causing harm or damage, often in a subtle way
example: Lack of sleep has a deleterious effect on both memory and mood.
origin: From Greek deleterios “noxious”, from deleisthai “to hurt”.

definition: Lacking a plan, purpose, or enthusiasm
example: After a few desultory attempts at conversation, they both returned to their phones.
origin: From Latin desultorius, from desultor, a circus rider who leaped from horse to horse, from desilire “to leap down”.

definition: Overflowing with cheerful energy and excitement
example: The ebullient crowd sang and danced in the streets after the final whistle.
origin: From Latin ebullire “to bubble out”, from e- “out” and bullire “to boil”.

definition: Lively, bubbly, and full of high spirits
example: Her effervescent personality made her the natural host of the morning show.
origin: From Latin effervescere “to boil up”, from ex- “out” and fervescere “to begin to boil”.

definition: Calmness and steady temper, especially under pressure
example: He took the news of the layoffs with remarkable equanimity.
origin: From Latin aequanimitas, from aequus “even” and animus “mind”.

definition: Understood by only a small group with special knowledge
example: The forum is full of esoteric debates about vintage synthesizer circuits.
origin: From Greek esoterikos “belonging to an inner circle”, from esotero “more within”, the comparative of eso “within”.

definition: Silly and pointless, often in a self-satisfied way
example: He kept making fatuous remarks while everyone else tried to solve the problem.
origin: From Latin fatuus, meaning “foolish”.

definition: Calm, happy, and peaceful, especially of a past time
example: She often talks about the halcyon days of her childhood by the sea.
origin: From Greek alkyon, “kingfisher”, a bird fabled to calm the sea while it nested around midwinter.

definition: Too great or intense to be put into words
example: Standing at the summit at sunrise, she felt an ineffable sense of peace.
origin: From Latin ineffabilis, from in- “not” and effari “to speak out”.

definition: Having a long-established habit that is unlikely to change
example: An inveterate traveler, he has visited more than ninety countries.
origin: From Latin inveteratus, from inveterare “to make old”, from vetus “old”.

definition: Completely clear and transparent, like still water
example: We could see every pebble at the bottom of the limpid mountain lake.
origin: From Latin limpidus, meaning “clear”.
